tag: Schools, workplaces & study — always in use
bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: notice that the exact same sentence frames ("I enjoy it because...", "I don't mind + -ing, but...") work whether you're a pupil, a student, or a working professional — learn the frame once, then just plug in whatever's true for you.

questions.text: Are you a student? What school do you go to?
questions.model: Yeah, I am. I'm currently studying Computer Science at Webster University in Tashkent. It's quite challenging at times, but I enjoy it because I've always been interested in technology and how things work.
usefulLanguage: be interested in how something works

questions.text: What's your favourite subject at school?
questions.model: I'd probably say Computer Science. I like subjects where I actually have to think and solve problems rather than just memorise a lot of information. It can be frustrating sometimes, but I find it really satisfying when I finally figure something out.

questions.text: Do you like your school?
questions.model: Yeah, overall, I do. I like the people there, and I think the atmosphere is pretty relaxed, so I feel comfortable studying there. Of course, there are a few things I'd change, but nothing major.
usefulStructure: There are a few things I'd change, but...

questions.text: What do you dislike about school?
questions.model: Probably the amount of work we sometimes get. There are periods when several assignments pile up at once, and then I have to spend most of my free time studying. I don't mind working hard, but I don't really enjoy having no time to switch off.

questions.text: What do you want to do after you finish school?
questions.model: Once I finish my studies, I'd like to get some experience in the tech industry, probably in software development or AI. I'm still figuring out exactly what I want to specialise in, though. For now, I just want to keep learning and see where it takes me.
usefulLanguage: figure out what I want to...
usefulStructure: Once + present simple, I'd like to + verb

questions.text: Are you a student? What are you studying?
questions.model: Yes, I am. I'm studying Computer Science, and most of what I'm doing at the moment is related to programming and problem-solving. It's not always easy, but I like the fact that there's usually a clear solution to work towards.
usefulStructure: Most of what I'm doing at the moment is + noun/-ing

questions.text: Why did you choose to study that subject?
questions.model: I chose it mainly because I've always been curious about technology. I also enjoy solving problems, and I like the idea of creating something from scratch rather than just using something that already exists. So I felt like Computer Science would suit me quite well.

questions.text: What do you like about your course?
questions.model: What I like most is that it's quite practical. We learn the theory, but we also have to use it to solve actual problems, which makes the classes more interesting. I also like the fact that I'm learning something that could be useful in my future career.

questions.text: Is there anything you dislike about your studies?
questions.model: Yeah, probably the workload. Around exam time, I can have several things to prepare for at once, so it gets a bit overwhelming. I sometimes end up putting off other things because I need to focus on my studies.

questions.text: What do you plan to do after you graduate?
questions.model: I'd like to start working in the tech industry, ideally in software development or something related to AI. At first, I'd probably focus on gaining experience and learning from people who are more experienced than me. Then, once I know the field better, I might think about starting my own projects or business.
usefulStructure: Once + present simple, I might + verb

questions.text: Do you work? What do you do?
questions.model: Yeah, I do. I work as an IELTS instructor at a learning centre, so I help students prepare for their exams, mainly by working on their speaking, writing, reading and listening skills. It can be quite demanding, but I really enjoy seeing students improve.

questions.text: Why did you choose that job?
questions.model: I got into teaching because I enjoy working with people, and I like explaining things in a way that's easy to understand. I also find it really rewarding when a student struggles with something at first but eventually gets it. So, yeah, I guess teaching was a pretty natural choice for me.

questions.text: What do you like about your job?
questions.model: Probably the best thing is seeing my students make progress. When someone comes into my class struggling with a particular skill and then improves over time, it's a really good feeling. I also like that every student is different, so I'm not doing exactly the same thing every day.

questions.text: Is there anything you dislike about your job?
questions.model: I'd say the workload can be a bit much sometimes. When I have a lot of students, there's usually quite a lot of preparation and marking to do, so it can take up most of my free time. I don't mind being busy, but I do need some time to relax and switch off.
usefulLanguage: the workload can be a bit much

questions.text: Do you think you'll stay in this job for a long time?
questions.model: I'm not sure, to be honest. I really enjoy teaching, so I can definitely see myself doing it for a few more years, but I'm also interested in technology and AI. I might eventually move into a different field, but I don't feel like I need to make that decision right now.

vocab.example: It's a stone's throw from the coast, actually.
It's turned into a sprawling suburb over the last decade.

vocab.meaning: a tightly connected group of people who know each other well
vocab.example: What I like most is that close-knit community feel.

vocab.meaning: a place seen as dull or unimportant
vocab.example: My grandparents live in a fairly quiet backwater, to be honest.
The town centre has undergone significant changes since I was a kid.

vocab.meaning: to have spent one's whole early life in a place
vocab.example: I was born and raised there, more or less.
It's known for its picturesque scenery, especially the riverside.
It's honestly a far cry from how I remember it as a kid.

bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: every answer here directly answers the specific question asked (size, duration, change, comparison) rather than reusing one generic hometown description — examiners notice immediately when a candidate gives the same rehearsed paragraph regardless of the actual question.

questions.text: Please describe your hometown a little.
questions.model: Sure — it's a fairly small city, a stone's throw from the coast actually, and I was born and raised there, more or less. It's got a nice mix of old and newer buildings, so it doesn't feel too modern or too run-down, if that makes sense.

questions.text: What is your hometown well-known for?
questions.model: Probably its picturesque scenery, if I'm honest, especially the riverside area, which draws a fair number of visitors in summer. There's also a fairly well-known market that's been running for decades, which people travel a surprising distance for.

questions.text: Do you like your hometown?
questions.model: I do, generally, yeah — I'd say what I like most is that close-knit community feel, everyone kind of knows everyone. It can occasionally feel a bit small, admittedly, but most of the time that closeness is honestly a nice thing to have.

questions.text: Is that a big city or a small place?
questions.model: It's fairly small, actually, more of a large town than a proper city, if I'm honest. You can walk pretty much everywhere within about twenty minutes, which I've come to really appreciate compared to bigger places.

questions.text: How long have you been living there?
questions.model: My whole life, pretty much, aside from a couple of years away for university in a different city. It was strange coming back at first, but it didn't take long to feel completely normal again.

questions.text: Do you think you will continue living there for a long time?
questions.model: Probably not forever, if I'm honest, though I'm not in any particular rush to leave either. Career opportunities might eventually pull me elsewhere, but for now I'm genuinely happy staying put.

questions.text: Would you like to live in the countryside in the future?
questions.model: Actually, yes, I think I would eventually — somewhere with a bit more picturesque scenery and considerably less noise than where I am now. It's not a priority right now, but I could see myself moving in that direction later in life.

questions.text: Have you ever lived in the countryside?
questions.model: Not really, no — the closest I've come is visiting my grandparents, who live in a fairly quiet backwater, to be honest. It's peaceful, though I don't think I could handle quite how remote it is on a permanent basis.

questions.text: Do you ever spend time in the countryside?
questions.model: Occasionally, yeah, mostly visiting family a couple of times a year. It's honestly a nice break from city life, even if it does get a little dull after more than a few days.

questions.text: What is the difference between living in the countryside and the city?
questions.model: I'd say pace, mainly — the countryside's obviously a lot slower, whereas the city's constantly changing, with something new happening practically every week. There's also just a lot more going on socially in the city, for better or worse.

questions.text: What do people living in the countryside like to do?
questions.model: From what I've seen, a lot of outdoor stuff, gardening, walking, that sort of thing, much more than people tend to do in the city. There's also a stronger sense of relying on neighbours for things, which you notice a lot less in urban areas.

questions.text: What do you like to do in the countryside?
questions.model: Mostly just relax, honestly, go for long walks and completely unplug from everything for a few days. It's one of the only places I genuinely switch my phone off, which says a lot, probably.

questions.text: How has your town changed over the last 20 years?
questions.model: Quite a lot, actually — it's undergone significant changes, and what used to be mostly farmland on the edge of town is basically a sprawling suburb now. It's honestly a far cry from how I remember it as a kid, for better and worse.

structure.label: Developing
phrases: what I like most about it is...

vocab.example: It's not huge, but there's plenty of space for the two of us.
It's got a cosy feel, especially in winter.
We moved into a fully furnished flat, which made things a lot easier.
The living room gets loads of natural light in the mornings.

vocab.meaning: a layout with few or no dividing walls
vocab.example: The kitchen and living room are open-plan, which I really like.

vocab.meaning: become comfortable in a new place
vocab.example: It didn't take long to settle in once we'd unpacked everything.

vocab.meaning: a party celebrating a new home
vocab.example: We had a housewarming not long after we moved in.

vocab.meaning: personalize a space so it feels comfortable and familiar
vocab.example: Small changes like that really help make it feel like home.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: notice short, natural contrast structures like "it's not huge, but there's plenty of space" — a simple "not X, but Y" pattern adds nuance to a Part 1 answer without needing complex grammar.

questions.text: Can you describe the place where you live?
questions.model: Sure — it's a two-bedroom flat with plenty of space for the two of us, on the third floor of a fairly modern building. Nothing too fancy, but it's comfortable, and it's in a pretty convenient location for getting into the city centre.

questions.text: What kind of housing accommodation do you live in?
questions.model: I live in a flat, actually, which came fully furnished when we first moved in, honestly making things a lot easier at the time. We've swapped out a few pieces since then, but most of the original furniture's still there.

questions.text: What do you like about your flat?
questions.model: Probably the natural light, if I'm honest — the living room faces east, so it's really bright first thing in the morning. It genuinely makes a difference to my mood, especially compared to my previous place, which felt fairly dark all day.

questions.text: Which room does your family spend most of the time in?
questions.model: Definitely the living room, mainly because it's open-plan with the kitchen, so everyone naturally ends up there while someone's cooking. We rarely all sit in separate rooms, if I'm honest, unless someone specifically wants some quiet.

questions.text: What can you see from the windows where you live?
questions.model: Mostly rooftops and a bit of a park in the distance, nothing too exciting, if I'm honest. On a clear day you can just about make out the hills on the edge of the city, which is a nice bonus.

questions.text: Do you prefer living in a house or a flat?
questions.model: A flat, personally, mainly for practical reasons — less maintenance overall, and it's got a cosy feel despite being fairly small. Houses are nice in theory, but the upkeep's genuinely not something I'm ready to take on yet.

questions.text: What would you like to change in your flat?
questions.model: Probably the kitchen, if I could — it's a bit outdated, and I'd love a proper open-plan layout eventually rather than the closed-off setup we've got now. Small changes like that really help make it feel like home, in my experience.

questions.text: What do you dislike about your flat?
questions.model: Honestly, just the lack of storage — there's plenty of space day to day, but storage is definitely lacking, especially in the bedrooms. We've had to get creative with shelving just to keep things from feeling cluttered.

questions.text: Who do you live with?
questions.model: Just my partner at the moment — it's a fairly small place, but that suits us fine for now. If anything, we'd like a bit more room eventually, once we're in a better position financially.

questions.text: How long have you lived there?
questions.model: About three years now — we had a housewarming not long after we moved in, actually. It didn't take long to settle in and make it feel like home, if I'm honest, though the first few months felt a bit strange.
